title: Pascal's Triangle II
description: Given an integer `rowIndex`, return the `rowIndex`-th row (0-indexed) of Pascal's triangle.
hints: Build the row iteratively from [1], updating each position from right to left so you don't overwrite a value you still need.

title: Length of Last Word
description: Given a string `s` consisting of words and spaces, return the length of the last word (a maximal substring of non-space characters).
hints: Strip trailing spaces, then walk backward from the end counting characters until the next space or the start of the string.

title: Contains Duplicate II
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return `true` if there are two distinct indices `i` and `j` such that `nums[i] == nums[j]` and `abs(i - j) <= k`.
hints: Track the most recent index at which each value was seen — if a repeat occurs within k of that recorded index, return true.

title: Contains Duplicate III
description: Given an integer array `nums` and integers `indexDiff` and `valueDiff`, return `true` if there exist two distinct indices `i` and `j` such that `abs(i - j) <= indexDiff` and `abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) <= valueDiff`.
hints: Bucket values into buckets of width (valueDiff + 1), keeping only a sliding window of indexDiff elements' buckets at a time.
A match exists if the current element's own bucket is occupied, or its neighboring buckets contain a value within valueDiff.

title: Intersection of Two Arrays II
description: Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return an array of their intersection, where each element appears as many times as it shows in both arrays (order doesn't matter).
hints: Count the frequency of every value in the smaller array, then scan the other array, emitting a value (and decrementing its count) whenever its count is still positive.

title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if there exists a triple of indices `i < j < k` such that `nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]`.
hints: Track the smallest value seen so far, and the smallest 'second value' seen so far that came after something smaller.
As soon as a third number comes along that's bigger than the second tracked value, a valid triplet exists.

title: First Missing Positive
description: Given an unsorted integer array `nums`, return the smallest missing positive integer.
hints: The answer is always between 1 and n+1 (where n is the array length) — anything outside that range is irrelevant.
Put every in-range value at its 'home' index (value v at index v-1) via swapping, then scan for the first index whose value doesn't match its home position.

title: Majority Element II
description: Given an integer array `nums` of size `n`, return every element that appears more than `⌊n / 3⌋` times, in any order.
hints: At most two values can appear more than n/3 times — extend Boyer-Moore voting to track two candidates and two counters simultaneously.
After finding the two candidates, verify each actually appears more than n/3 times (a final counting pass).

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
description: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove duplicates so each unique value appears at most twice, preserving relative order. Return the resulting array.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: Keep a write pointer; only append the current value if fewer than 2 copies of it have been written so far (compare against the value 2 positions back in the result).

title: Patching Array
description: Given a sorted integer array `nums` and an integer `n`, add patches (any positive integers) so that every number in the range `[1, n]` can be formed as a sum of some subset of the array. Return the minimum number of patches required.
constraints: nums is sorted in ascending order.
hints: Track 'reach', the largest value provably coverable as [1, reach] so far.
If the next array element is beyond reach+1, you must patch with (reach+1) itself, doubling your reach; otherwise consume the array element and extend reach by its value.

title: Summary Ranges
description: Given a sorted unique integer array `nums`, return the smallest sorted list of ranges that exactly covers all the numbers in the array. Each range is formatted `"a->b"` if `a != b`, or just `"a"` if `a == b`.
constraints: nums is sorted and consists of unique values.
hints: Scan through, extending the current range while consecutive values keep incrementing by 1; close and record the range whenever that streak breaks.

title: Missing Ranges
description: Given a sorted unique integer array `nums` and a range `[lower, upper]`, return the smallest sorted list of ranges that exactly covers every number in `[lower, upper]` that is missing from `nums`. Each range is formatted `"a->b"` if `a != b`, or `"a"` if `a == b`.
hints: Walk through the conceptual sequence lower, lower+1, ..., upper alongside nums, and whenever there's a gap between the last covered value and the next present number (or upper), record that gap as a range.

title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
description: Given an integer `n`, return the number of trailing zeroes in `n!`.
hints: Trailing zeroes come from factors of 10 = 2*5, and factors of 5 are always the bottleneck (there are always more 2s than 5s).
Count how many multiples of 5, 25, 125, ... are <= n, and sum them.

title: Nim Game
description: You and a friend play Nim: starting with `n` stones, players alternate removing 1-3 stones, and whoever removes the last stone wins. You go first. Return `true` if you can guarantee a win, assuming optimal play from both sides.
hints: Whenever n is a multiple of 4, whatever you take (1-3), your opponent can always take enough to bring the total removed per round back to 4, eventually forcing you to face 0 stones on your turn.
So the answer is simply: n is NOT a multiple of 4.

title: Bulls and Cows
description: You are playing Bulls and Cows with a friend: they picked a 4-digit `secret` number, and you guessed `guess`. Return a hint in the form `"xAyB"` where `x` is the number of bulls (correct digit, correct position) and `y` is the number of cows (correct digit, wrong position).
constraints: secret and guess consist of digits only.
hints: Count bulls first (matching digit at matching position), then for the remaining non-bull digits, count how many digit values are shared between secret and guess (capped by the smaller count of each digit) — that total is the cows.

title: Additive Number
description: An additive number is a string whose digits can form an additive sequence: at least 3 numbers, no leading zeros (except the number 0 itself), where each number from the third onward is the sum of the previous two. Given a string `num` of digits, return `true` if it's an additive number.
hints: Backtrack by trying every possible split for the first two numbers (respecting the no-leading-zero rule), then greedily check whether the rest of the string continues the additive pattern exactly.

title: Verify Preorder Serialization of a Binary Tree
description: A binary tree can be serialized as a comma-separated preorder traversal string where `"#"` marks a null node. Given a string `preorder`, return `true` if it is a valid serialization of some binary tree, without reconstructing the tree.
constraints: preorder consists of digits, commas, and '#'.
hints: Track available 'slots' for children, starting at 1 (for the root). Each non-null node consumes one slot and creates two new ones; each null node just consumes one slot.
The serialization is valid if slots never go negative and end at exactly 0 after processing every token.

title: Interval List Intersections
description: Given two lists of closed intervals `firstList` and `secondList`, each sorted by start time and pairwise disjoint within their own list, return the intersection of the two interval lists.
hints: Use two pointers, one per list. Two intervals overlap when the later start is <= the earlier end — record that overlap, then advance whichever interval ends first.

title: Valid Number
description: Given a string `s` (with no leading or trailing whitespace), return `true` if it represents a valid decimal number, such as "2", "0089", "-0.1", "+3.14", "4.", "-.9", "2e10", "-90E3", or "6e-1". A number must have at least one digit, an optional single leading sign, at most one decimal point, and an optional exponent part ('e' or 'E' followed by an optional sign and one or more integer digits, no decimal point allowed in the exponent).
constraints: s contains only digits, '+', '-', '.', 'e', 'E', and letters.
hints: This is cleanly expressed as a regular expression: an optional sign, then either digits with an optional decimal point (with digits on at least one side), then an optional exponent (e/E, optional sign, one or more digits).

title: Minimum Window Subsequence
description: Given strings `s` and `t`, return the minimum contiguous substring `w` of `s` such that `t` is a subsequence of `w` (characters of `t` appear in `w` in order, not necessarily contiguous). Return an empty string if no such window exists.
hints: Scan forward through s to find where t is first fully matched as a subsequence, ending at some index.

Then scan backward from that ending index to find the tightest starting point that still contains t as a subsequence — that gives one candidate window. Repeat scanning forward from just after the previous match to find all candidates and keep the shortest.

title: Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters
description: Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, return the length of the longest substring that contains at most `k` distinct characters.
hints: Slide a window, tracking a running count of each character inside it; shrink from the left whenever the number of distinct characters exceeds k.

title: Longest Substring with At Most Two Distinct Characters
description: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest substring that contains at most two distinct characters.
hints: This is the same sliding-window-with-a-distinct-character-cap technique as the general K-distinct version, just fixed at k=2.

title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
description: Given a string `s` and an array of strings `words` (all the same length), return the starting indices of every substring in `s` that is a concatenation of every word in `words` exactly once, in any order.
hints: Every word has the same length, so a valid window has a fixed total length (wordLen * len(words)); check each possible starting index by breaking the window into wordLen-sized chunks and verifying the chunk multiset matches the words multiset exactly.

title: Palindrome Permutation
description: Given a string `s`, return `true` if some permutation of it could form a palindrome.
hints: A string can be rearranged into a palindrome exactly when at most one character has an odd frequency count.

title: Longest Palindrome
description: Given a string `s` of letters, return the length of the longest palindrome that can be built using those letters (case-sensitive; not all letters need to be used).
constraints: s consists of lowercase and/or uppercase English letters only.
hints: Every character with an even count can be fully used in matching pairs on both sides of the palindrome.
For characters with an odd count, use one less than their count (as pairs), and you may place a single extra character in the very middle if any odd-count character exists.

title: Sentence Screen Fitting
description: Given a `sentence` (array-joined into one string, words separated by single spaces) and a screen with `rows` rows and `cols` columns, the sentence repeats itself and is typed left to right, top to bottom, wrapping only at word boundaries. Return the number of times the given sentence can be fully displayed on the screen.
constraints: sentence consists of lowercase English letters and spaces.
hints: Conceptually glue the sentence's words together with a single space, wrapping infinitely — simulate one row at a time, using modular arithmetic over the joined-sentence-with-trailing-space length to jump forward quickly instead of placing word by word.

title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
description: Given a string `s` containing letters and parentheses, remove the minimum number of invalid parentheses to make the string valid. Return every possible valid result (with that minimum number of removals), in any order.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters and '(', ')'.
hints: BFS level by level: at each level, try removing every single character from every string in the current level's set, checking each result for validity.
Stop at the first level where at least one valid string is found — that level uses the minimum number of removals, so collect every valid result found at exactly that level.

title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
description: Given a string `expression` of numbers and operators (`+`, `-`, `*`), return every possible result from computing all the different ways to group numbers and operators via parentheses, in any order (duplicate values from different groupings are all kept).
hints: Recursively split the expression at every operator: everything to the left and right of that operator can independently be computed in every possible way, then combined with that operator.
A substring with no operators is a base case — it's just a single number.

title: Split Array into Fibonacci Sequence
description: Given a string `num` of digits, return any valid Fibonacci-like sequence (at least 3 numbers, each fitting in a 32-bit signed integer, no leading zeros except the number 0 itself, each number the sum of the previous two) formed by splitting `num`, or an empty array if none exists. When multiple valid splits exist, this returns the one found by preferring the shortest possible first number, then the shortest possible second number.
hints: Backtrack trying every valid (no-leading-zero, 32-bit-fitting) length for the first two numbers, shortest first, then greedily check whether the rest of the string continues the Fibonacci pattern exactly.

title: Length of Longest Fibonacci Subsequence
description: Given a strictly increasing array of positive integers `arr`, return the length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence in it (length >= 3, each term the sum of the previous two), or `0` if none exists.
hints: dp[(a, b)] = length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence ending with the pair (a, b).
For every pair of indices (i, j) with i < j, check if arr[j] - arr[i] exists earlier in the array (as arr[k], k < i) — if so, dp[(arr[i], arr[j])] = dp[(arr[k], arr[i])] + 1 (or 3 if no prior entry).

title: IPO
description: You have initial capital `w` and can complete at most `k` distinct projects (each `profits[i]` with required minimum capital `capital[i]`, only startable if your current capital is at least that requirement). Completing a project adds its profit to your capital. Return the maximum capital you can have after completing at most `k` projects.
hints: Sort projects by required capital. At each step, push every project now affordable (given current capital) into a max-heap keyed by profit, then greedily take the most profitable one available.
Repeat k times (or until no project is affordable).

title: Single-Threaded CPU
description: Given `tasks` where `tasks[i] = [enqueueTime, processingTime]`, a single-threaded CPU processes at most one task at a time, always choosing (when idle) the available task with the shortest processing time, breaking ties by the smallest original index. Return the order (original indices) in which tasks are processed.
hints: Sort tasks by enqueue time. Simulate time passing: whenever the CPU is idle, push every task that has become available into a min-heap keyed by (processingTime, index), then process the top of the heap.
If no task is available yet, jump the clock forward to the next task's enqueue time instead of idling forever.

title: Remove Covered Intervals
description: Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [li, ri]`, remove every interval that is covered by another interval in the list (interval `[a, b]` is covered by `[c, d]` if `c <= a` and `b <= d`). Return the number of remaining intervals.
hints: Sort by start ascending, and for equal starts, by end descending (so a longer interval starting at the same point comes first).
Scan through, tracking the maximum end seen so far — an interval is covered exactly when its end doesn't exceed that running maximum.

title: Video Stitching
description: You are given `clips` where `clips[i] = [starti, endi]` represents a sub-clip of a video. Return the minimum number of clips needed to cover the entire video from time `0` to `time`, or `-1` if impossible.
hints: Greedily, like Jump Game II: for the currently covered range up to some point, look among all clips that start within that range, and pick whichever extends the covered end the farthest.

title: Sliding Window Median
description: Given an integer array `nums` and a window size `k`, return the median of each sliding window of size `k` as it moves from the start to the end of the array.
hints: For each window position, sorting just that window (or maintaining a sorted structure incrementally) gives the median directly — the middle element for odd k, or the average of the two middle elements for even k.

title: Optimize Water Distribution in a Village
description: There are `n` houses. You can either build a well in house `i` for `wells[i-1]` cost, or connect two houses with a pipe (`pipes[j] = [house1, house2, cost]`). Return the minimum total cost to supply water to every house.
hints: Treat building a well in house i as a pipe of that cost from a virtual node 0 to house i.
Then this is a Minimum Spanning Tree problem over n+1 nodes — run Kruskal's algorithm (sort all edges by cost, union-find to avoid cycles).

title: Merge K Sorted Arrays
description: Given `lists`, an array of `k` sorted integer arrays, merge them all into a single sorted array and return it.
hints: Use a min-heap holding the current smallest unconsumed element from each list (tagged with its list and position), repeatedly popping the overall smallest and pushing that list's next element.

title: Numbers At Most N Given Digit Set
description: Given a sorted array of unique digit-strings `digits` and an integer `n`, return how many positive integers less than or equal to `n` can be built using only digits from `digits` (each digit may be used as many times as needed).
hints: Count all valid numbers with fewer digits than n outright (each digit position freely chosen: len(digits)^length possibilities).

For numbers with exactly the same digit count as n, walk n's digits left to right: at each position, count how many available digits are strictly smaller than n's digit here (those fix the rest of the number freely), then continue only if n's own digit is itself available; add 1 at the end if you matched n exactly all the way through.

title: Bus Routes
description: Given `routes` where `routes[i]` is the sequence of bus stops that the `i`-th bus repeats forever, and integers `source` and `target`, return the minimum number of buses you must take to travel from `source` to `target`, or `-1` if impossible.
hints: Build a map from each stop to the list of bus routes serving it.

BFS over ROUTES (not stops): starting from every route serving source, each BFS layer represents boarding one more bus, expanding to every route reachable by sharing a stop with a route already visited.

title: Cut Off Trees for Golf Event
description: You are given a `forest` grid where `0` is an obstacle, `1` is walkable ground, and any value greater than `1` is a tree of that height. Starting at `(0, 0)`, cut every tree in order from shortest to tallest, moving 4-directionally. Return the total number of steps to cut all trees, or `-1` if any tree is unreachable.
hints: Sort every tree position by height first — that fixes the visiting order.
BFS from your current position to each next tree in turn, summing up the shortest-path steps; fail immediately if any tree is unreachable.

title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
description: Given an undirected connected graph of `n` nodes as `graph` (adjacency lists), return the length of the shortest path that visits every node at least once, starting and ending at any nodes (nodes/edges may be revisited).
hints: BFS over states of (current node, bitmask of visited nodes), starting simultaneously from every node with only itself visited.
The answer is the fewest steps to reach any state where the bitmask has every bit set.

title: Swim in Rising Water
description: Given an `n x n` grid where `grid[i][j]` is the elevation at that cell, at time `t` you may swim between adjacent cells only if both have elevation at most `t`. Starting at `(0, 0)`, return the minimum time until you can reach `(n-1, n-1)`.
constraints: grid is a permutation of [0, n^2 - 1].
hints: This is Dijkstra-flavored: from the start, always expand into the reachable cell with the smallest elevation next (a min-heap), and track the maximum elevation crossed so far along the best path.
The answer is the maximum elevation crossed by the time you first reach the destination.

title: The Maze
description: A ball is in a `maze` grid (`0` empty, `1` wall) and rolls in a chosen direction until it hits a wall (it doesn't stop at intermediate empty cells). Given the `start` and `destination` positions, return `true` if the ball can stop exactly at the destination.
hints: From each stopping position, simulate rolling in all 4 directions until hitting a wall to find the next stopping position — BFS/DFS over these stopping positions as graph nodes.

title: The Maze II
description: A ball is in a `maze` grid (`0` empty, `1` wall) and rolls in a chosen direction until it hits a wall. Given `start` and `destination`, return the shortest total rolling distance for the ball to stop exactly at the destination, or `-1` if impossible.
hints: Same rolling-simulation graph as The Maze, but now edges are weighted by how far each roll travels — Dijkstra's algorithm (a min-heap of cumulative distance) finds the shortest total distance to the destination.

title: Flower Planting With No Adjacent
description: You have `n` gardens (labeled 1 to n) and a list `paths` of bidirectional paths between them (each garden has at most 3 paths). Using 4 types of flowers, assign each garden a flower type such that no two connected gardens share the same type. Return any valid assignment as an array (1-indexed types).
constraints: Each garden has at most 3 paths.
hints: Since each garden touches at most 3 neighbors, 4 flower types always suffice — greedily assign each garden the smallest flower type not already used by its already-assigned neighbors.

title: Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid
description: Given an `m x n` grid where `grid[i][j]` (1-4) indicates a fixed direction arrow, moving along the indicated direction costs 0, and moving any other direction costs 1 (changing that cell's arrow), return the minimum cost to make a path from `(0, 0)` to `(m-1, n-1)`.
hints: This is a 0-1 BFS: following the cell's own arrow direction costs 0, any other direction costs 1.
Use a deque, pushing 0-cost moves to the front and 1-cost moves to the back, to process cells in true shortest-cost order.

title: Path With Minimum Effort
description: Given a `heights` grid, you travel from `(0, 0)` to `(rows-1, cols-1)`, moving 4-directionally. Your route's effort is the maximum absolute difference in heights between two consecutive cells along it. Return the minimum possible effort.
hints: This is Dijkstra's algorithm where 'distance' is redefined as the maximum edge weight (height difference) along the path so far, rather than a sum — always expand into the reachable cell with the smallest such 'effort so far' next.

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the maximum result of `nums[i] XOR nums[j]` for any pair of indices.
hints: Build the answer bit by bit from the most significant bit down: greedily assume each new bit can be set, and check (via a hash set of number prefixes seen so far) whether some pair actually achieves that prefix.

title: Concatenated Words
description: Given an array of distinct strings `words`, return every string in `words` that is a concatenation of at least two shorter words from `words` (each usable multiple times), in any order.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
All strings in words are unique.
hints: For each word, check if it's word-breakable into 2 or more pieces using the OTHER words in the set (a Word Break variant that additionally requires at least two pieces).
A word set (excluding the word being tested) works well as the dictionary for a per-word DP check.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
description: Given an `m x n` integer matrix, return the length of the longest strictly increasing path (moving 4-directionally).
hints: DFS from each cell, memoizing the longest increasing path starting there — since values strictly increase along any path, there's no cycle to worry about, so memoization is safe.

title: Dungeon Game
description: A knight starts at the top-left of a `dungeon` grid (negative values are damage, positive are healing) and must reach the bottom-right, moving only right or down. The knight dies if health drops to 0 or below at any point. Return the minimum initial health needed to guarantee reaching the destination alive.
hints: Work backward from the destination: dp[r][c] = minimum health needed upon ENTERING cell (r, c) to survive the rest of the path.
dp[r][c] = max(1, min(dp[r+1][c], dp[r][c+1]) - dungeon[r][c]).

title: Cherry Pickup
description: Given an `n x n` grid where `1` is a cherry, `-1` is a thorn (impassable), and `0` is empty, collect the maximum cherries by walking from `(0, 0)` to `(n-1, n-1)` moving only right or down, then back to `(0, 0)` moving only left or up (a cherry can only be counted once).
hints: A round trip is equivalent to two people walking simultaneously from (0,0) to (n-1,n-1), both only moving right or down.
Since both people take the same number of steps at any point, one position (r2) determines the other (c2 = r1+c1-r2) — memoize on (r1, c1, r2).

title: Super Egg Drop
description: You are given `k` identical eggs and a building with `n` floors. There exists a critical floor such that an egg breaks if dropped from that floor or above, and doesn't break below it. Return the minimum number of moves needed to determine the critical floor with certainty in the worst case.
hints: Reformulate: with m moves and k eggs, how many floors can you certainly distinguish? dp[m][eggs] = dp[m-1][eggs-1] + dp[m-1][eggs] + 1 (drop here: eggs-1 remain if it breaks, eggs remain if it survives, plus the floor itself).
Find the smallest m for which dp[m][k] >= n.

title: Race Car
description: Your car starts at position 0 with speed +1 on an infinite track. Given a sequence of instructions 'A' (accelerate: position += speed, speed *= 2) or 'R' (reverse: speed becomes -1 or +1, position unchanged), return the minimum number of instructions to reach exactly position `target`.
hints: Let n be the number of consecutive accelerations that would land exactly on or past target. Either drive exactly to 2^n - 1 then reverse and solve the remaining (smaller) subproblem, or drive n-1 accelerations, reverse, drive m accelerations back, reverse again, and solve from there for every reasonable m.
Memoize on the remaining distance to reach.

title: Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden
description: There is a garden of length `n` (positions `0` to `n`), with a tap at every integer position; tap `i` (with range `ranges[i]`) waters the interval `[i - ranges[i], i + ranges[i]]`. Return the minimum number of taps needed to water the full garden `[0, n]`, or `-1` if impossible.
hints: Convert each tap into an interval, then this is exactly the Jump Game II / Video Stitching greedy pattern: repeatedly extend your covered range as far as possible using taps that start within the currently reachable area.

title: K Inverse Pairs Array
description: An inverse pair in a permutation of `1` to `n` is a pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `arr[i] > arr[j]`. Given `n` and `k`, return the number of permutations of `1` to `n` that have exactly `k` inverse pairs, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Build permutations of 1..i one size at a time: inserting the new largest element at a given position adds a controllable number (0 to i-1) of new inverse pairs.
dp[i][j] = sum of dp[i-1][j-x] for x in 0..i-1 — use a running prefix sum (sliding window) to compute this efficiently rather than a nested loop.

title: Number of Music Playlists
description: You have `n` distinct songs and want to create a playlist of length `goal`, using every song at least once, where a song can only be replayed if at least `k` other songs have played since its last play. Return the number of possible playlists, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: dp[i][j] = number of playlists of length i using exactly j unique songs so far.
Each new song added at position i is either brand new ((n-j+1) choices) or a replay of an already-used song that's past its cooldown (j-k choices, if positive).

title: Stone Game II
description: Alice and Bob play a game with piles of stones, `piles`, taking turns (Alice first). On a turn, a player takes the first `x` piles (`1 <= x <= 2M`, where `M` starts at 1 and afterward becomes `max(M, x)` for the next turn). Both play to maximize their own total. Return the maximum number of stones Alice can get.
hints: Precompute suffix sums. dp(i, M) = the best score the CURRENT player can get from piles[i:], given the current M.

If 2M covers all remaining piles, take them all. Otherwise try every x from 1 to 2M, and the current player's score is (suffix sum from i) minus whatever the opponent achieves optimally afterward — maximize over x.

title: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones
description: There are `stones` piles in a row. In one move you may merge exactly `k` consecutive piles into one, costing the total number of stones in those piles. Return the minimum total cost to merge all piles into one, or `-1` if impossible.
hints: A merge is only possible if (n - 1) is divisible by (k - 1) — check this first.

dp[i][j] = minimum cost to merge piles i..j down as far as possible; split at every mid point reachable in steps of (k-1), and if the full range i..j can collapse to exactly one pile, add the full range's sum.

title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `counts` where `counts[i]` is the number of elements to the right of index `i` that are strictly smaller than `nums[i]`.
hints: Coordinate-compress the values, then use a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree): process nums from right to left, and for each value, query how many smaller values have already been inserted before inserting the current one.

title: Reverse Pairs
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the number of reverse pairs — pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]`.
hints: Use a merge-sort-based divide and conquer: after recursively sorting both halves, count cross-pairs (a from the left half, b from the right half, a > 2*b) using two pointers before merging.

title: Count of Range Sum
description: Given an integer array `nums` and two integers `lower` and `upper`, return the number of range sums that lie within `[lower, upper]` inclusive (a range sum is the sum of `nums[i..j]` for `i <= j`).
hints: Build the prefix sum array; a range sum for nums[i..j] equals prefix[j+1] - prefix[i].
Use merge-sort-based divide and conquer over the prefix sums, counting valid (i, j) pairs across the two halves before merging (similar in spirit to Reverse Pairs).

title: Unique Paths III
description: Given a grid where `1` marks the starting square, `2` the ending square, `0` empty squares, and `-1` obstacles, return the number of paths from start to end that walk over every non-obstacle square exactly once.
constraints: grid contains exactly one 1 and exactly one 2.
hints: Backtrack from the start, tracking how many empty squares remain to be visited; only count a path as valid when you reach the end with exactly zero squares left unvisited.

title: Minimum Difficulty of a Job Schedule
description: Given `jobDifficulty` and an integer `d`, split the jobs (in order) into `d` non-empty contiguous groups (one group per day), where a day's difficulty is the maximum job difficulty that day. Return the minimum possible total difficulty across all days, or `-1` if there aren't enough jobs for `d` days.
hints: dp[i][j] = minimum total difficulty to schedule the first i jobs over j days.
For each dp[i][j], try every possible last-day split point k, taking the max difficulty of jobs k+1..i as that day's cost, added to dp[k][j-1].

title: Tallest Billboard
description: You have steel rods with lengths `rods`, and want to weld some into two support pillars of EQUAL height (using each rod fully in at most one pillar, or not at all). Return the largest possible pillar height, or `0` if you can't build any pillars of positive height.
hints: Track a map from (taller pillar height - shorter pillar height) to the maximum achievable shorter-pillar height for that difference.
For each rod, it can extend the taller side, or the shorter side (which may flip which side is taller) — update every entry in the map accordingly. The answer is the map's value at difference 0.

title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
description: Given `startTime`, `endTime`, and `profit` arrays describing `n` jobs, where you may only work non-overlapping jobs, return the maximum total profit achievable.
hints: Sort jobs by end time. dp[i] = best profit using only the first i jobs (in this sorted order).
For each job, either skip it (dp[i-1]) or take it (its profit plus the best dp value among jobs that ended at or before this job's start — find that via binary search on end times).

title: Number of Ways to Stay in the Same Place After Some Steps
description: You have a pointer starting at index 0 on an array of length `arrLen`. In each of `steps` moves, you may move the pointer left, right, or leave it in place, as long as it never goes outside the array bounds. Return the number of ways to be back at index 0 after exactly `steps` moves, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: The pointer can never usefully go further than steps/2 positions away and still return, so cap the reachable range at min(arrLen - 1, steps).
dp[step][pos] = number of ways to be at pos after that many steps; transition by trying left/stay/right at each step.

title: Combination Sum III
description: Find all valid combinations of exactly `k` distinct numbers from `1` to `9` that sum to `n`, where each combination's numbers are used at most once. Return every combination, in any order.
hints: Backtrack through digits 1-9 in increasing order, tracking how many are chosen and their running sum, pruning branches that exceed n or can't possibly reach k digits.

title: Palindrome Permutation II
description: Given a string `s`, return every distinct palindromic permutation of it, in any order (an empty array if none exist).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only.
hints: A palindrome is only possible if at most one character has an odd count.
Build the first half from each character's (count // 2) copies via backtracking permutation, then mirror it (with the single odd character, if any, in the middle) to form each full palindrome.

title: Flip Game II
description: You and a friend play a game with a string `currentState` of '+' and '-' characters, taking turns flipping two consecutive '++' into '--'. The game ends when a player cannot make a move (and that player loses). Return `true` if the starting player can guarantee a win with optimal play.
hints: Try every possible move (flipping some "++" to "--"); the current player wins if any resulting state is a LOSING state for the opponent (i.e., canWin on that resulting state returns false).
Memoize on the state string to avoid recomputation.

title: Sudoku Solver
description: Given a partially filled `9 x 9` Sudoku `board` (0 marks an empty cell, guaranteed to have a unique solution), return the fully solved board.
constraints: The given board has a unique solution.
hints: Backtrack cell by cell: for each empty cell, try digits 1-9, checking the row/column/3x3-box constraints, placing the first digit that works and recursing, undoing it if no full solution follows.

title: Android Unlock Patterns
description: Android phones have a 3x3 unlock pattern grid (dots numbered 1-9). A valid pattern visits between `m` and `n` dots, never revisiting a dot, and if it moves directly between two dots that have another dot exactly in between them, that middle dot must have already been visited. Return the number of valid unlock patterns of length between `m` and `n` inclusive.
hints: Precompute, for every pair of dots, which 'skip' dot (if any) must already be visited to jump directly between them.

Backtrack building patterns, only allowing a jump to a new dot if it's adjacent (no skip needed) or its required skip dot was already visited. Exploit symmetry: patterns starting at corners are equivalent to each other (multiply by 4), and similarly for edges (multiply by 4); only the center is unique.

title: Strobogrammatic Number
description: A strobogrammatic number looks the same when rotated 180 degrees (looked at upside down). Given a string `num` representing an integer, return `true` if it is strobogrammatic.
hints: Only 0, 1, 6, 8, 9 can appear in a strobogrammatic number (6 and 9 rotate into each other).
Two pointers from both ends: check that each pair of digits are 180-degree rotation partners of each other.

title: Strobogrammatic Number II
description: Given an integer `n`, return all strobogrammatic numbers with exactly `n` digits, in any order (no leading zeros, unless the number is exactly "0").
hints: Build outward from the middle: for a core of length n-2, wrap it with each valid rotation-symmetric digit pair (00, 11, 69, 88, 96), skipping a leading 0 pair unless it's the only digit.
Base cases: length 0 is the empty string, length 1 is '0', '1', '8'.

title: Confusing Number
description: A confusing number is one that, when rotated 180 degrees, becomes a DIFFERENT valid number (0, 1, 6, 8, 9 rotate to 0, 1, 9, 8, 6 respectively; 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 become invalid when rotated). Given a number `n`, return `true` if it is confusing.
hints: Rotate each digit using the valid mapping (failing immediately if any digit has no valid rotation), then compare the rotated number to the original — they must differ.

title: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
description: Given an integer `n`, return the count of all numbers `x` with `0 <= x < 10^n` where every digit of `x` is unique.
hints: Count how many unique-digit numbers have exactly k digits (no leading zero) using permutation counting: 9 choices for the first digit, then 9, 8, 7, ... for subsequent digits.
Sum these counts for k = 1 to n, plus 1 for the number 0.

title: Valid Word Square
description: Given an array of strings `words`, return `true` if they form a valid word square (the `k`-th row and `k`-th column read the same string, for every valid `k`).
hints: For every cell (r, c) within bounds of words[r], check that words[c][r] exists and matches words[r][c] — and that reading column c doesn't run past where row r's characters stop being defined.

title: Max Points on a Line
description: Given an array of `points` where `points[i] = [xi, yi]`, return the maximum number of points that lie on the same straight line.
hints: For each point, compute the slope to every other point (as a reduced fraction to avoid floating-point error), grouping points by slope — the largest group plus the anchor point gives a candidate line.

title: Valid Triangle Number
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the number of triplets that can form the sides of a valid triangle with non-zero area (chosen from the array's elements, order doesn't matter).
hints: Sort the array. Fix the largest side at index k, then use two pointers i, j on the smaller sides (i < j < k): if nums[i] + nums[j] > nums[k], every index between i and j also works with j fixed, so count them all at once and move j down; otherwise move i up.

title: 132 Pattern
description: Given an array of integers `nums`, return `true` if there exists a 132 pattern — indices `i < j < k` such that `nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]`.
hints: Scan from right to left, maintaining a monotonic decreasing stack and tracking the largest value ever popped from it (a valid candidate for the '2' in the pattern).
If the current element is smaller than that tracked value, a valid '1' has been found completing the pattern.

title: Couples Holding Hands
description: There are `n` couples sitting in `2n` seats in a row, given by `row` (each value is a person's id; couple `2i` and `2i+1` are partners). Return the minimum number of swaps so that every couple sits side by side.
hints: Process seat pairs left to right: if the person in the next seat isn't the current person's partner, find the partner elsewhere and swap them into place.
Each such swap fixes exactly one couple, so just count the swaps performed.

title: Constrained Subsequence Sum
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the maximum sum of a non-empty subsequence such that for every pair of consecutive chosen indices `i` and `j` (`i < j`), `j - i <= k`.
hints: dp[i] = best subsequence sum ending exactly at index i = nums[i] + max(0, best dp value among the previous k indices).
A monotonic decreasing deque of (dp value, index) gives that sliding-window maximum efficiently.

title: Jump Game V
description: Given an array `arr` and an integer `d`, from index `i` you may jump to index `i+x` or `i-x` (for `1 <= x <= d`, within bounds) only if every index strictly between `i` and the destination has a strictly smaller value than `arr[i]`, and the destination itself has a strictly smaller value than `arr[i]`. Return the maximum number of indices you can visit starting from any single index (counting the start).
hints: Process indices in increasing order of their value — by the time you process index i, every index it could jump to has already been fully resolved (since jumps only go to strictly smaller values).
dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over every valid jump destination j from i.

title: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended
description: Given `events` where `events[i] = [startDay, endDay]`, you can attend one event per day, attending any single day within that event's range. Return the maximum number of distinct events you can attend.
hints: Process days in order. Each day, add every event that has become available (start <= today) to a min-heap keyed by end day, discard any expired events (end < today) from the heap top, then greedily attend whichever available event ends soonest.

title: Car Fleet
description: There are `n` cars heading to the same destination `target` along a one-lane road, given by `position` and `speed`. A car catching up to a slower car ahead forms a fleet (traveling together at the slower speed, never passing). Return the number of distinct fleets that will arrive at the destination.
hints: Sort cars by starting position, closest to target first. For each car, compute the time it would take to reach target alone.
Scanning from closest to farthest, a car merges into the fleet ahead if its arrival time is <= the time of the fleet currently forming; otherwise it starts a new fleet.

title: Score After Flipping Matrix
description: Given a binary matrix `grid`, you may choose any row or column and flip every value in it. After any number of such flips, each row is read as a binary number; return the maximum possible sum of all rows' binary values.
hints: To maximize value, every row should start with a 1 (its most significant bit) — flip any row that starts with 0.

After fixing all row-leading-bits to 1, for each column independently, flip it only if that increases the count of 1s in that column (more 1s in a column is always better since flipping is column-wide).

title: Maximum Earnings From Taxi
description: You drive a taxi on a road with `n` points (1 to n). Given `rides` where `rides[i] = [starti, endi, tipi]`, picking up that ride earns `endi - starti + tipi` and takes you from `starti` to `endi` (you can only carry one passenger at a time, but may skip any distance for free). Return the maximum total earnings.
hints: This is weighted interval scheduling: dp[i] = best earnings achievable using only points up to i.
Group rides by their end point; at each point, dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], max over rides ending at i of dp[start] + profit).

title: Maximum Number of Non-Overlapping Subarrays With Sum Equals Target
description: Given an array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the maximum number of non-overlapping (non-empty) subarrays whose sum equals `target`.
hints: Greedily scan left to right, tracking prefix sums seen. Whenever the current prefix sum minus target has been seen before, that's a valid subarray ending here — take it immediately and reset the seen-prefix-sums set (since subarrays can't overlap).

title: Count Nice Pairs in an Array
description: Given an array `nums`, return the number of nice pairs — indices `i < j` such that `nums[i] + rev(nums[j]) == nums[j] + rev(nums[i])`, where `rev(x)` reverses the digits of `x`. Return the count modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Rearranging the equation: nums[i] - rev(nums[i]) == nums[j] - rev(nums[j]) — so group numbers by the value (num - rev(num)) and count pairs within each group.

title: Minimum Operations to Reduce X to Zero
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `x`, in one operation you may remove the leftmost or rightmost element of `nums`, subtracting its value from `x`. Return the minimum number of operations to reduce `x` to exactly `0`, or `-1` if impossible.
hints: Reduce this to: find the longest contiguous subarray (in the middle) whose sum equals (total sum of nums) - x — the removed prefix+suffix is the complement.
Slide a window over the array, shrinking from the left whenever the window sum exceeds that target, tracking the maximum valid window length found.

title: Brick Wall
description: Given a rectangular `wall` where `wall[i]` is a list of brick widths for row `i` (all rows the same total width), draw one vertical line from top to bottom, crossing the minimum number of bricks (a line along an edge between bricks doesn't count as crossing). Return that minimum number of crossed bricks.
hints: For each row, compute the running cumulative edge positions (excluding the final edge at the wall's full width).
Count how many rows share each interior edge position; the best line goes through the position shared by the most rows, crossing every other row's brick.

title: Teemo Attacking
description: Given a non-decreasing array `timeSeries` of attack timestamps and an integer `duration` (each attack poisons the target for exactly `duration` seconds, and re-attacking during an active poison simply resets the timer rather than stacking), return the total number of seconds the target is poisoned.
constraints: timeSeries is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: For each attack after the first, add the smaller of duration or the gap to the next attack — if the next attack lands within the current poison window, the window just resets instead of extending fully.

title: Can Place Flowers
description: Given a binary array `flowerbed` (0 empty, 1 planted, no two adjacent 1's) and an integer `n`, return `true` if `n` new flowers can be planted without violating the no-adjacent-flowers rule.
hints: Scan through, greedily planting in any empty plot whose left and right neighbors (treating out-of-bounds as empty) are also empty, incrementing a counter each time.

title: Maximum Average Subarray I
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the maximum average value of any contiguous subarray of length `k`.
hints: Use a fixed-size sliding window: compute the first window's sum directly, then slide by subtracting the element leaving and adding the element entering, tracking the maximum sum seen.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal
description: You have an array `arr` of length `n` where `arr[i] = (2 * i) + 1` for `0 <= i < n`. In one operation, you may pick two indices and increment one by 1 and decrement the other by 1. Return the minimum number of operations to make all elements equal.
hints: The array is symmetric around its middle value, so the target equal value is just the average.
Sum the distance from each of the first half's elements to the target — that total equals the answer (the second half mirrors it exactly).

title: Shortest Word Distance
description: Given an array of strings `wordsDict` and two different strings `word1` and `word2` that both exist in the array, return the shortest distance between their occurrences (the minimum absolute difference of their indices).
constraints: word1 and word2 both appear in wordsDict.
hints: Scan through once, tracking the most recent index seen for each of the two words, and updating the minimum distance whenever both have been seen.

title: Battleships in a Board
description: Given an `m x n` matrix `board` where `1` represents part of a battleship (horizontal or vertical, never touching another ship) and `0` is water, return the number of battleships on the board.
hints: Count only the 'top-left' cell of each ship: a cell with value 1 whose cell above and cell to the left are both not part of a ship (out of bounds or 0) — that's exactly one count per ship.

title: Champagne Tower
description: You stack champagne glasses into a triangular tower with `100` rows (row `r` has `r+1` glasses). One cup is poured with `poured` units at the top; whenever a glass overflows (holds more than 1 unit), the excess splits equally to the two glasses below it. Return how full (0 to 1) the glass at `(query_row, query_glass)` ends up.
hints: Simulate row by row: track how much liquid arrives at each glass (which can exceed 1), and pass exactly max(0, (amount - 1) / 2) down to each of the two glasses below.
The final fullness of a query glass is min(1, amount received).

title: Minimum Time Visiting All Points
description: Given an array `points` where `points[i] = [xi, yi]`, return the minimum time (in seconds) to visit every point in the given order, moving one unit per second in any of the 8 directions (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal).
hints: Between two consecutive points, the fastest route uses diagonal moves as much as possible, then straight moves — so the time is Chebyshev distance: max(|dx|, |dy|).
Sum this over every consecutive pair of points.

title: Number of Good Pairs
description: Given an array of integers `nums`, return the number of good pairs — indices `i < j` such that `nums[i] == nums[j]`.
hints: Count the frequency of each value; a value appearing c times contributes c*(c-1)/2 good pairs.
